Read together, they yield four sequenced stages, each pinned to a rising rung of the taxonomy and each equipped with a distinct AIGC entry point. The Learning stage handles knowledge input. Micro-lecture videos and interactive animations, generated with AIGC support, deliver foundational concepts in a form that keeps early extraneous demands low 38 . Comparable media designs in art and design programmes-augmented-reality frameworks for practice-based education 39 and animation-based problem-solving materials 40 -indicate that the delivery format itself carries part of the instructional burden. Instructor-student interaction here stays largely one-directional, and the output is judged by a recall-and-comprehension rubric. The Thinking stage lifts the target objective toward analysis: AI-driven problem scenarios prompt learners to interrogate what they have absorbed, forcing conceptual reconstruction rather than passive acceptance 1 . Assessment shifts to the quality of reasoning traces students leave behind. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 In the Applying stage, skill transfer takes over. Students turn to open-source animation software to realize concrete schemes, moving from understanding to execution 3 . The teacher's role becomes that of a troubleshooter, and deliverables are scored against technical fidelity and completion. The Creating stage sits at the apex of the ladder, where an AIGC co-creation platform hosts original animation projects 10 . Here human-machine collaboration is genuinely reciprocal, and originality, coherence, and expressive intent form the evaluation criteria. Figure 2 traces the full activity sequence and tool-embedding nodes across the four stages. The escalation across stages is deliberate rather than incidental. Learning targets recall and comprehension; Thinking moves to analysis; Applying demands transfer into production; and Creating asks for synthesis and original expression. Each stage also hands something forward, since the artefact and the competence produced at one stage become the entry condition for the next: a student who has already interrogated a script arrives at modelling with a plan rather than a blank scene. The four stages do not carry equal weight in assessment. Final work is judged against the Creating stage, while the earlier stages are assessed formatively, which keeps the evaluative emphasis on original output without leaving the preparatory work unmonitored 35 . Eligibility required current enrolment in the core animation curriculum and no prior exposure to structured AIGCbased instruction, since the intervention presumes a comparable starting point in generative-tool familiarity 3 . Two intact classes served as the sampling frame, and allocation was made at class level, one class being assigned at random to the experimental condition and the other to the control. Randomising whole classes respected existing timetables, a pragmatic choice common in classroom-based research 28 ; with only two clusters, however, it cannot equate the groups in the way individual randomisation would, so the design is quasi-experimental and any class-level difference remains confounded with condition. The study is educational rather than clinical: participants were healthy students, the intervention was instructional, and all outcomes were educational measures. Approval from the institutional review board was obtained, and every participant gave written informed consent before baseline testing. The experimental group received the AIGC-driven LTAC integrated animation instruction, whereas the control group followed conventional animation teaching built around demonstration and guided practice 38 . Baseline equivalence was examined beforehand on sex ratio, age, prior animation experience, cognitive load, and creative thinking pretest scores. Categorical variables were compared with 𝜒𝜒 2 tests and continuous ones with independent-samples t tests; none of the comparisons was significant at p < 0.05, which is consistent with baseline equivalence without establishing it 30 . Table 2 reports these comparisons. As Table 2 indicates, the two groups did not differ appreciably on any measured attribute before instruction. That similarity makes a preexisting-difference account less plausible for the effects reported later, though with two clusters it cannot exclude unmeasured class-level differences 23 . The intervention ran for twelve weeks at four class hours per week, forty-eight class hours in total, and the same instructor taught both groups so that delivery style was held constant. Cognitive load was captured with a subjective rating instrument that separates intrinsic, extraneous, and germane subscales and records each item on a nine-point Likert continuum. The single-item mental-effort rating introduced by Paas provided the response format 42 , while the item content of the three subscales followed the differentiated instrument of Leppink and colleagues, which recovers the three load types as distinct components 43 . Splitting the construct this way matters for the present design, since the hypothesised pathways treat the three loads as functionally distinct rather than interchangeable 34 . The battery used here therefore followed the published Chinese adaptation in task format and scoring logic, with item stems revised for an adult sample and re-checked by translation and backtranslation. analysis.discussion: Why did the AIGC-driven model pull extraneous load down while pushing germane load up? The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The same logic extends to redundancy. Conventional animation instruction often forces learners to process the same content through several channels at once-verbal explanation layered over manual sketching-whereas the generative pipeline lets each channel do distinct work, trimming the duplicated processing that inflates extraneous load 13 . Freed capacity does not simply vanish, though. Fig. 9 Heatmap of standardized path coefficients linking the three cognitive load dimensions to the four creative thinking facets, with color intensity encoding effect magnitude and direction. Fig. 8 Scatter plot of creative thinking composite scores against intrinsic cognitive load, overlaid with the fitted quadratic curve. The vertex falls at a moderate load value, approximately 5.9 on the ninepoint scale, which is the pattern an inverted-U association implies. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 The generative activities in the Thinking and Creating stages demand that students evaluate, curate, and reassemble machine output, which is exactly the kind of effortful schema-building that germane load names 23 . The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . items.abstract_text: The launch of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds created an unusual allocation problem: 10 intermediaries offered nearly the same underlying exposure, yet their flows diverged sharply. This paper is a focused reanalysis of the fund-flow and Reddit panel introduced by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]. It does not present the dataset, text measures, BrandScore or the baseline sentiment-by-visibility association as new. Instead, it asks what the established association reveals about the division between category demand and intermediary choice. The contribution consists of three interpretive emphases applied to estimates already reported by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]: within-date differences across funds as evidence about allocation, asymmetry across the conditional flow distribution and variation across market states. The pairwise flow-sensitivity formulation makes the allocation interpretation explicit. In the previously reported two-way fixed-effects model, common daily shocks are absorbed and the sentiment-by-visibility coefficient is identified from differences in issuer visibility among funds facing the same Bitcoin news. The coefficient is positive, the direct visibility effect changes sign between large-redemption and large-creation states and the interaction appears less consistently during stressed markets. The Driscoll–Kraay and issuer-bootstrap checks apply to the baseline coefficient (2.930), not the two-way fixed-effects coefficient (3.802), for which those checks were not conducted. The evidence is thus an associative allocation regularity, not a causal social-media effect: differences in issuer visibility are consistent with different flows across financial wrappers conditional on common category sentiment.

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) in gastrointestinal endoscopy has focused on computer-aided detection (CADe) for recognition errors; AI addressing endoscope motion, coverage, workflow, and skill – collectively kinematic analysis – has not been systematically synthesized. AIM To map kinematic AI evidence across eight predefined domains and assessed its quality relative to CADe and surgical AI. METHODS MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE-OVID, Cochrane, and IEEE Xplore were searched following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist (CRD420261320279). Studies applying AI to kinematic data in gastrointestinal endoscopy were eligible. Risk of bias used Cochrane Risk of Bias 2, Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2, and PROBAST + AI; certainty of evidence used GRADE. RESULTS Fifty-eight studies were included. Evidence generation was asymmetric: (1) Randomized controlled trial ratio approximately 5:1 (> 40 vs 8); (2) Patient ratio approximately 4:1 (> 27000 vs approximately 6200); (3) Annual publication ratio approximately 12:1; and (4) ≥ 6 vs 0 regulatory approvals favoring diagnostic AI. Withdrawal speed monitoring and coverage/blind-spot mapping reached moderate GRADE certainty, but all 8 randomized controlled trials were from China and 6 of 8 used the ENDOANGEL platform. The remaining six domains have not reached moderate certainty: (1) Workflow recognition and skill assessment are approaching clinical readiness; and (2) Autonomous navigation, robotic control, simultaneous localization and mapping/three-dimensional reconstruction, and instrument tracking remain at the engineering stage. Comparison with surgical AI indicated that the gap reflects ecosystem-level factors – absence of open datasets, benchmarking challenges, and regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI – rather than technical immaturity. CONCLUSION Kinematic AI addresses exposure errors that CADe cannot correct and has shown additive benefit alongside CADe. Two domains are ready for geographically diverse validation; six remain at the engineering stage. Priorities are open datasets, benchmarking infrastructure, and dedicated regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI.

This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana.
reading.findings: The results showed universal access to smartphones (99%), while 71% had access to a laptop. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). Second, interaction on digital platforms occurs at multiple levels and at different physical places (e.g. home, school setting) for some purposeful outcomes. Positive outcomes through GenAI use reflect gains (manifested as strengths) whilst the negative experiences Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:37204 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5 14 and outcomes create digital anxieties (afflictions). Third, GenAI use within the higher education context is constrained or limited by institutional-level factors (macro-level) such as policies on GenAI use, access to digital platforms and type of engagement. Thus, institutional factors mediate and shape adult learners' use of GenAI within this context. As such, adult learners' experiences of the extent to which their level of need and satisfaction is met through GenAI use reveal their state of well-being/wellness. Furthermore, both results highlight that within the higher education context, adult learners’ use of GenAI on a variety of digital platforms to perform academic and non-academic tasks is pervasive. Multiple digital connectivity at different places fosters a continuous cycle of constantly and actively creating and recreating their digital experiences, leading to cognitive and affective gains as well as embodied strains. Through such a process, they develop several coping systems which are mostly culturally embedded to counteract and adjust to the unpleasant physical afflictions. In sum, adult learners' digital well-being occurs through these nested multiple layers of influence (at the individual, meso and macro-levels), and is sustained by the powerful functionalities In addition, the results reveal that adult learners' positive gains with GenAI usage moderately influenced their cognitive, affective, and psychosocial well-being. For example, the qualitative arm of the study showed that adult learners appreciated the powerful functionalities of GenAI through enhanced efficiency in learning, but expressed psychological strain and apprehension. While it is true that GenAI tools like ChatGPT can enhance cognitive tasks, for instance, by making problem-solving activities easier, improving self-efficacy for task resolution and enhancing the quality and originality of solutions83, blind usage does not foster critical thinking and problem-solving, which are essential for academic and lifelong success15. Furthermore, the study found that some adult learners experienced minimal effects on their physical well-being as a result of GenAI usage, necessitating the development of self-adaptive coping mechanisms to alleviate the negative impacts of their digital experiences. Inferring from the unified ecological framework8, which illustrates a linkage between physical and digital domains influencing DWB when interacting with AI, the results imply that while GenAI usage may confer mental and emotional advantages, these are accompanied by modest but consistent reports of adverse bodily effects. Past studies have suggested that GenAI can reduce stress by streamlining tasks or creating a stress-free and emotionally supportive learning environment42,43,84, but excessive use of such technologies can lead to heightened anxiety, burnout, and sleep disturbance85. reading.interpretation: This study examined the association between generative AI dependence and medical students' clinical reasoning and tested whether critical thinking statistically accounted for part of this association. The results showed that generative AI dependence was negatively associated with critical thinking, whereas critical thinking was positively associated with clinical reasoning. After critical thinking was included, the direct association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning remained significant, suggesting that critical thinking accounted for only part of this association. AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking, but high AI literacy did not eliminate this negative association. Given that this study used an observational, three-wave time-lagged design and did not include baseline measures, the results can only reflect associations among variables rather than strict causal relationships; pre-existing individual differences, reverse or reciprocal associations, and unmeasured time-varying confounders cannot be ruled out. In addition, the outcome in this study was self-reported Clinical Reasoning as reflected by diagnostic thinking disposition, rather than objectively demonstrated clinical reasoning performance, diagnostic accuracy, or patient safety outcomes. In summary, this study suggests that medical education should focus on fostering calibrated AI use, critical thinking, and AI literacy, rather than simply restricting AI use; future intervention studies are still needed to verify whether such educational strategies can actually improve medical students' clinical reasoning.
reading.limitations: This study has some limitations. First, although a time-lagged design was used to reduce common method bias, this study was not experimental and therefore cannot establish causal relationships. Future studies should use longitudinal observation, randomized trials, or instructional programs to examine the long-term associations between generative AI dependence and the development of clinical reasoning. Second, most of the sample consisted of medical students. Regional differences, institutional characteristics and other factors may limit the generalizability of these results to medical education. Future studies should determine whether similar findings generalize to learners in other fields, practicing clinicians, and healthcare training systems worldwide. No unmatched identification codes, duplicate identification codes, or item-level missing values were present in the retained dataset. Thus, retention from T1 to T2 and from T2 to T3 was 100%, no participants were lost to follow-up after the T1 cohort was locked. The final analytical sample comprised 648 complete three-wave cases, and the valid response rate met social science research standards. Secondly, this study selected undergraduate medical students with experience using generative AI as the study population for two main reasons. First, medical students need to process large amounts of professional knowledge, case information, and evidence within limited study time. GenAI can substantially reduce the time and effort required for information searching and organization. Medical students therefore have a relatively strong need to use AI tools. The numbers of students from the first to fifth academic years were 77, 139, 163, 160, and 109, respectively. Fourth-and fifth-year students accounted for 269 participants, or 41.5% of the sample. Formal clinical reasoning instruction began in year 3, and clinical exposure increased progressively from year 3 to year 5. These contextual characteristics were considered when interpreting the findings and assessing generalizability. Fourth, the moderated mediation results further show that AIrelated risks in medical education are shaped by the interaction of "user characteristics" and "patterns of use". Students with lower AI literacy showed a stronger negative association between AI dependence and critical thinking, which was in turn associated with lower clinical reasoning. Students with higher AI literacy are more likely to retain the information of verification and human supervision, thus reducing the negative indirect effect. Medical AI education should therefore focus less on tool proficiency and more on calibrated reliance and professional judgment. Fifth, in terms of the overall effect structure, AI literacy is positively correlated with both critical thinking and clinical reasoning, and it also moderates the negative path associated with AI dependence; thus, AI literacy extends beyond technical ability. It may reflect a type of "meta-technological ability" that helps students determine when to use AI, how to evaluate its output, and when human reasoning should be employed. As AI models continue to improve, this ability will be needed more. The more expert-like AI-generated answers become, the more students need to recognize when their own use is developing into inappropriate dependence. Taken together, these findings partially confirm, extend, and differ from previous research on active AI engagement, critical thinking, and potentially problematic AI use. Gerlich (9) reported that AI tool use was associated with cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Tian and Zhang (18) found that AI dependence was associated with lower critical thinking. The present study extends these findings by linking generative AI dependence to a professional outcome, clinical reasoning, through critical thinking. The findings differ from studies showing that LLM assistance can improve immediate diagnostic performance under structured conditions, such as Roemer et al. (4) and Brügge et al. (5) . Those studies mainly examined student-plus-AI performance, whereas the present study examined self-reported diagnostic thinking disposition without AI assistance. The findings are also consistent with Goh et al. (6) , which did not find that access to GPT-4 automatically improved physicians' diagnostic reasoning. Thus, the present results confirm some prior concerns, extend them to medical students and clinical reasoning, and differ from studies focused on immediate assisted performance.
analysis.discussion: This study examined the association between generative AI dependence and medical students' clinical reasoning and tested whether critical thinking statistically accounted for part of this association. The results showed that generative AI dependence was negatively associated with critical thinking, whereas critical thinking was positively associated with clinical reasoning. After critical thinking was included, the direct association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning remained significant, suggesting that critical thinking accounted for only part of this association. AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking, but high AI literacy did not eliminate this negative association. Given that this study used an observational, three-wave time-lagged design and did not include baseline measures, the results can only reflect associations among variables rather than strict causal relationships; pre-existing individual differences, reverse or reciprocal associations, and unmeasured time-varying confounders cannot be ruled out. In addition, the outcome in this study was self-reported Clinical Reasoning as reflected by diagnostic thinking disposition, rather than objectively demonstrated clinical reasoning performance, diagnostic accuracy, or patient safety outcomes. In summary, this study suggests that medical education should focus on fostering calibrated AI use, critical thinking, and AI literacy, rather than simply restricting AI use; future intervention studies are still needed to verify whether such educational strategies can actually improve medical students' clinical reasoning.
analysis.limitations: This study has some limitations. First, although a time-lagged design was used to reduce common method bias, this study was not experimental and therefore cannot establish causal relationships. Future studies should use longitudinal observation, randomized trials, or instructional programs to examine the long-term associations between generative AI dependence and the development of clinical reasoning. Second, most of the sample consisted of medical students. Regional differences, institutional characteristics and other factors may limit the generalizability of these results to medical education. Future studies should determine whether similar findings generalize to learners in other fields, practicing clinicians, and healthcare training systems worldwide. Third, generative AI dependence, critical thinking, AI literacy, and clinical reasoning were all measured by self-report. Although the above measures have good reliability and validity, the observed associations may still be subject to social desirability and other biases. Future studies should combine self-reported data with case studies and standardized objective clinical examination (OSCE) scores and other performance indicators. Finally, generative AI is developing rapidly. Differences in model capabilities, interaction modes, and application settings may be associated with students' experiences and cognitive responses. However, the present study did not collect detailed information on which specific GenAI systems participants used or their purposes of use. Because different systems may involve different capabilities, interaction patterns, and levels of output reliability, the sample should not be assumed to be homogeneous with respect to AI exposure. This limits the generalizability of the findings and prevents us from examining whether the observed associations differ across specific GenAI tools or usage purposes. Future studies should therefore explore the differences among AI tools and specific types of medical learning tasks, and should collect detailed information on the types of GenAI systems used, the purposes and task contexts of use, and the frequency of use for each system. In addition, the CFA and subsequent hypothesis tests were conducted using the same analytical sample rather than an independent validation sample. Independent replication would provide a stronger test of measurement stability. The very high reliability coefficients for AI literacy and clinical reasoning, together with their relatively high mean inter-item correlations, also suggest that some item overlap may be present. Future studies should evaluate whether shorter forms can retain construct breadth while improving measurement efficiency.

items.abstract_text: Purpose In the AI era, digital transformation has become essential for enterprises to adapt as complex systems to uncertain business environments. In this work, we aim to analyze the evolutionary dynamics of AI-driven enterprise digital transformation (EDT), focusing on its evolution and impact on enterprise performance from a system cybernetics perspective. Design/methodology/approach We employ evolutionary dynamics analysis grounded in game theory to model the EDT process, and perform an econometric and empirical analysis on a sample of Chinese A-share-listed enterprises from 2009 to 2023. The approach encompasses heterogeneity analysis, moderation effect models, such as testing enterprise environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and market concentration, and threshold effect analyses. Findings The evolutionary dynamics analysis finds that increasing the risk-averse benefits of traditional enterprises and reducing the additional benefit coefficient would hinder EDT. Increasing the investment of technology enterprises in internal resource restructuring accelerates the transformation process. Empirically, AI significantly contributes to EDT. ESG positively moderates the relationship between AI and EDT, while market concentration exerts a negative moderating effect. Furthermore, AI and EDT show an inverted U-shaped trend when R&D intensity exceeds a specific threshold, while a U-shaped trend is observed when enterprise performance exceeds a specific threshold. Originality/value In this work, we uncover the complex, non-linear cybernetic feedback loops, such as U-shaped and inverted U-shaped, and boundary conditions, such as ESG and market concentration for AI-driven EDT, offering systemic strategies for enterprises adapting to the digital ecosystem.

analysis.methods: This study employed a quantitatively driven mixed-methods design with an embedded qualitative component. Quantitative data constituted the primary strand of the study and were used to assess teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs before and after participation in the professional development program. Qualitative data were obtained from two open-ended questionnaire items administered at the same measurement points and were used to contextualize and further interpret patterns observed in the quantitative findings. The qualitative component was therefore not implemented as a separate follow-up phase developed after preliminary quantitative analysis. Instead, quantitative and qualitative data were collected within the same broader assessment procedure and integrated during interpretation. The open-ended responses provided additional insight into how teachers described the role of students’ social-emotional well-being and the potential use of AI in educational research. This design enabled numerical changes in the measured constructs to be considered alongside changes in participants’ reported perceptions and intended practices. The two strands were integrated primarily at the interpretation stage and in the development of the empirically informed conceptual model. The research process comprised two complementary components: a quantitative component based on the structured questionnaire and an embedded qualitative component based on the two open-ended questions administered at the same measurement points. In the quantitative component, the structured questionnaire was used to assess chemistry teachers’ research competence, their reported practices of monitoring students’ social-emotional well-being, their perceptions of students’ achievement emotions, and their readiness to integrate AI technologies into research and pedagogical practice. The quantitative data were used to describe the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs, as well as to examine the relationships among these predefined measures. The embedded qualitative component involved analysis of participants’ responses to the two open-ended questionnaire items using qualitative content analysis. The purpose of this qualitative component was to provide additional insight into teachers’ professional needs, perceived challenges in conducting educational research, and their views on the opportunities and limitations of AI-assisted research. Integration of the quantitative and qualitative findings informed the development of a study-derived conceptual model illustrating the relationships among educational inquiry, teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices, AI-supported research practices, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. The study was conducted during the 2025–2026 academic year in public secondary schools in the South Kazakhstan region. A total of 105 chemistry teachers participated in the study. Participants were selected using the purposive sampling method. The main selection criteria were the participants’ currently teaching chemistry in a general secondary school, teaching experience, and informed voluntary consent to participate in the study. The sample comprised teachers with diverse levels of professional experience, qualification categories, and teaching backgrounds, allowing the researchers to examine research competence across a broad range of professional contexts and career stages. Data were collected using a theory-informed questionnaire developed for the present study. The questionnaire constructs and item content were informed by established theoretical frameworks and previously published instruments addressing teachers’ research competence, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and the educational use of artificial intelligence. Items were adapted to the context of in-service chemistry teachers and aligned with the constructs specified a priori in the study framework. analysis.discussion: The present study examined changes in chemistry teachers’ research competence following participation in an AI-supported professional development program integrating teacher inquiry, social-emotional monitoring, and AI. The combined quantitative and qualitative findings showed that research competence can be understood as a multidimensional and integrated professional construct encompassing inquiry, evidence interpretation, reflective practice, and data-informed pedagogical decision-making. Statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across the measured constructs, while the qualitative findings indicated corresponding shifts in teachers’ perceptions and reported practices. These patterns suggest that participation in the program was associated with greater integration of educational research into teachers’ instructional practice and with increased attention to evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. Regarding the first research question, the descriptive findings characterized the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related constructs predefined in the questionnaire. Among these measures, teachers’ research competence showed the lowest mean item score, whereas comparatively higher baseline scores were observed for social-emotional monitoring and perceptions of achievement emotions. Correlation analysis further revealed statistically significant positive associations among research competence, research engagement, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and readiness to use AI. These relationships indicate that the measured constructs are associated within teachers’ broader professional practice; however, they should not be interpreted as evidence that the present study empirically established the internal dimensional structure of research competence. The constructs were specified a priori on the basis of the theoretical framework and previous research rather than derived through exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis. This pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts that conceptualize research competence as embedded within a broader system of methodological, reflective, and professional capacities ( Ivanenko et al., 2015 ; Matjašič and Vogrinc, 2025 ). In the present study, the observed associations suggest that research competence is related to teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices and readiness to use AI, while the relatively lower baseline score for research competence indicates a potential area for further professional development. The relatively modest baseline scores for research competence further suggest that although many teachers possess a theoretical understanding of educational research, they continue to experience difficulties translating this knowledge into systematic classroom-based inquiry. This interpretation is consistent with the findings reported by Gümüşok et al. (2024) . The second research question focused on teachers’ perceptions of the role of students’ social-emotional well-being in educational research and pedagogical decision-making. The qualitative findings revealed a shift in how participants conceptualized this information following the program. Before participation, teachers tended to describe students’ emotional well-being primarily as a general factor influencing academic achievement and motivation. After the program, participants more frequently emphasized systematic observation, monitoring, and the potential use of social-emotional information as contextual evidence for classroom inquiry and pedagogical decision-making. These findings align with the work of Ng et al. (2025) , who highlighted the importance of social-emotional data for evidence-informed educational decision-making. Similarly, Li and Qian (2025) showed the impact of teacher social-emotional competence on the quality of education. Importantly, the present findings suggest that teachers increasingly recognized the potential of AI to support research-related activities, including the future organization and interpretation of social-emotional information within classroom inquiry. However, the present study did not directly test AI-based analysis of student-level social-emotional data. With respect to the third research question, statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across all measured constructs following participation in the AI-supported professional development program. The standardized within-participant changes were approximately medium in magnitude (Cohen's d z = 0.47–0.63). The largest standardized pre–post change was observed for teachers’ research competence (d_z = 0.63), which was the primary developmental focus of the program. Given the absence of a comparison group, however, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that the program itself caused the observed improvements. Rather, they indicate that improvements in the measured constructs occurred during the period of program participation. Because AI was embedded within a multicomponent professional development program, the observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI. They should instead be interpreted as changes occurring during participation in the integrated program as a whole. The qualitative findings further illustrate the changes in the patterns of teachers’ reported perceptions of AI. Prior to the intervention, AI was predominantly viewed as a tool for searching scientific literature, translating or formatting texts. Following participation in the program, however, teachers increasingly described AI as a methodological partner capable of supporting multiple stages of the research process, including research planning, development of data collection instruments, statistical analysis, interpretation of empirical findings, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that AI-supported tools can contribute to teachers’ professional activities, although the specific applications examined across previous studies differ from those investigated here. Choi et al. (2023) similarly reported that teachers used an AI chatbot for lesson planning, classroom management, and subject-matter support. The present findings do not demonstrate AI-based analysis of students’ social-emotional data. Rather, they indicate that participants increasingly recognized potential research-related applications of AI. AI-supported analysis of student-level social-emotional data should therefore be regarded as a prospective application of the proposed conceptual framework that requires direct empirical testing. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the study was conducted with a relatively small sample of 105 in-service chemistry teachers from a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to teachers of other subject areas, educational contexts, or national education systems. Second, the study employed a single-group pre-test/post-test design without a comparison or control group. Consequently, although statistically significant improvements were observed following participation in the professional development program, these changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the program. Alternative explanations, including repeated-measurement effects, maturation, concurrent professional experiences, or other contextual influences during the study period, cannot be ruled out. Future studies employing controlled or quasi-experimental comparative designs are therefore needed to establish whether the observed changes can be specifically attributed to the intervention. Third, the majority of the data were derived from self-report questionnaires and participants’ reflective responses, which may be influenced by social desirability and self-perception biases. Fourth, the study assessed only short-term changes following the professional development program, and the sustainability of the observed improvements in research competence, social-emotional monitoring practices, and AI readiness was not examined. Future research should therefore include larger and more diverse samples, longitudinal follow-up, comparison groups, and objective indicators such as classroom observation, research products, or student-related outcomes. In addition, the study did not collect direct student-level social-emotional measures or apply AI-based models to analyse or predict individual students’ social-emotional states. Therefore, conclusions regarding AI-supported social-emotional analysis are limited to teachers’ perceptions, reported practices, and the conceptual possibilities identified within the proposed framework. Future studies should test these applications directly using ethically collected student-level data and appropriately validated analytical methods. Moreover, the multicomponent nature of the professional development program prevents the independent contribution of AI from being separated from the effects of research-methods instruction, classroom inquiry, collaborative reflection, and other digital tools. Future studies using factorial, component-comparison, or controlled designs are needed to determine the specific contribution of AI-supported activities.

analysis.methods: The empirical foundation of this study necessitates a corpus that authentically captures the ideological tug-of-war within global AI safety governance. Consequently, we constructed a specialized comparative corpus representing the two dominant institutional factions: regulatory authorities (supranational entities and sovereign states) and regulated entities (leading technology corporations holding market monopolies). At the macro-level of data collection, representative and authoritative texts were assembled to ensure comprehensive coverage. The regulatory sub-corpus (Corpus B) comprises macro-policy frameworks, notably the U.S. Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, and Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework and so on. Conversely, the corporate sub-corpus (Corpus A) encompasses technical standards and safety frameworks from industry leaders, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Huawei and so on. Collectively, these carefully clipped texts constitute a targeted, domain-specific corpus of contemporary institutional AI safety discourse, offering a focused empirical basis for analyzing the discursive tension between political regulation and technological capital. To mitigate the inherent genre asymmetry between the macrosocietal focus of regulatory policy documents and the highly technical, engineering-centric nature of corporate manuals, a rigorous, protocol-driven thematic clipping strategy was operationalized. Rather than conducting a crude full-text comparison, which would inevitably skew the statistical data toward irrelevant technical jargon in Corpus A, the compilation process employed a targeted extraction protocol. Specifically, the tables of contents and structural headers of all corporate documents were systematically screened to isolate core chapters directly addressing risk mitigation mechanisms, responsibility demarcations, and safety compliance protocols. To strictly operationalize this thematic clipping and guarantee that no relevant discursive information was inadvertently missed, the excluded technical sections (e.g., mathematical proofs, computational benchmarking, and software code snippets) underwent a secondary validation protocol. This involved automated concordancing with a predefined lexical set of governance-related keywords (e.g., safety, ethics, risk, compliance, liability), which empirically confirmed the total absence of epistemic or regulatory claims within the omitted structural data. Because this study investigates the linguistic construction of safety governance as a sociopolitical phenomenon rather than the mathematical validity of the AI models, the exclusion of purely computational segments is theoretically justified. This rigorous thematic alignment maximizes functional and semantic parity between the opposing camps and eliminates structural noise without compromising the integrity of the critical discourse analysis. Following these procedures, the finalized bipartite corpus yielded highly balanced datasets (see Table 1 ), with Corpus A totaling 116,082 tokens and Corpus B reaching 116,636 tokens, thereby securing a robust quantitative baseline for subsequent analysis.

Current AI chatbots have more intelligent interactive characteristics than previous intelligent cus- tomer service systems, can provide anthropomorphic interaction based on intelligent analysis of user data, and can achieve more diversified and richer functional services. At the same time, with the improvement of natural language processing, big data analysis, and platform intelligent services, the positioning of AI chatbots in cus- tomer service is also gradually transforming from auxiliary tools into core service carriers. Therefore, this study aims to focus on AI chatbots on Meituan’s instant retail platform, explore the actual user experience of Genera- tion Z, and propose corresponding user experience enhancement strategies. This is also relatively consis- tent with the findings of this study. According to the AHP weight analysis results, requirement types such as quick access to feature, humanized AI interaction, personalized avatars for AI chatbots, and interface design optimiza- tion had relatively high weight values. At the same time, the requirement weights of intelligent emotion-aware interaction, AI personalized recommendation, and smart content recommendation were also relatively high. This indicates that Generation Z users’ actual experiences with AI chatbots may be related to dimensions such as emo- tional interaction and personalized services. In addition, existing studies have suggested that privacy statements and user trust may affect user satisfaction. In this study, privacy transparency was classified as one-dimensional quality in the KANO model evaluation, while the AHP weight analysis also showed that service trust and assur- ance needs was one of the important requirements. This result is relatively consistent with existing studies, indi- cating that information transparency and user trust are important factors in the user experience of AI chatbots. Compared to existing research, this study has also yielded new findings in its conclusions. Existing research suggests that AI chatbots can effectively enhance satisfaction and user experience by providing instant responses, accurately addressing user needs, and improving service quality. First, through empirical research, this study classified, screened, and ranked the experience pain points and further experience needs of Generation Z users when using AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. These experi- ence needs have rarely been mentioned in previous studies. These new findings can provide new evidence for the subsequent construction of a theoretical system of AI chatbot user experience. Second, previous user experience studies have focused more on user experience issues related to interface touch interaction and physical interac- tion. This study further extends the research object to the exploration of interaction behaviors between humans and intelligent agents, which can further enrich the user experience perspective in the field of human–computer interaction and supplement empirical research on user experience between humans and intelligent agents. In addition, it can also supplement empirical findings on the user experience of Generation Z users when using AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.

reading.findings: Recently, there have been many studies abroad on artificial intelligence-aided language learning. A meta-analysis of the 28 studies and 70 effect sizes found that chatbot-assisted language learning has a moderate positive effect compared with non-chatbot conditions, and this effect is moderated by educational level, language proficiency, interface design and interactional capability [1] . Therefore, AI cannot achieve good results on its own; it is only effective when matched with suitable teaching plans and students. Natural language processing tools can be used to conduct interactive and personalised exercises for learning specialised vocabulary. A case study showed that the learners' understanding of sustainability-related vocabulary increased significantly, and they could use the new words in context [11] . In pronunciation training, a speech-based ChatGPT intervention showed that learners continuously improved in multiple recordings and maintained the gains in a delayed posttest; thus, AI interaction can promote both immediate performance and long-term learning [12] . AI-simulated interlocutors in interactional competence can generate preferred responses, repair strategies and culturally appropriate closing remarks, but different models vary in the clarity and pragmatism of scaffolding [13] . Additionally, the impact of AI-generated stories and gamified learning on vocabulary retention and engagement has also been studied [14] . Together, these studies indicate that the effectiveness of AI is related to task authenticity, high-quality feedback and deep learner involvement.
reading.interpretation: In this paper, the five directions of research for generative AI-assisted language learning are: cognitive mechanisms, theoretical contradictions, empirical evidence, application design and ethical governance. According to the study, the main goal of artificial intelligence in education is not to substitute teachers but to enlarge the scope of language learning by reducing students' extraneous cognitive load, providing on-demand scaffolding, generating contextualized materials and offering timely feedback. The conflict between generative linguistics and generative AI is not absolute; rather, at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program, the two are in harmony. Based on the above empirical research, chatbots have provided some help for language learning, but this advantage varies according to the level of study and the design of interaction. Based on the above analysis, this paper puts forward a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools to build a closed-loop system of assessment, planning, practice, feedback, updating and community support. Finally, this paper presents some ethical problems of AI language education, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance and educational disparity, and proposes a multi-stakeholder governance system to address these issues. Future research can explore the long-term effects of AI on minority and marginalized languages, pragmatics, cultural adaptation, and thus move from "instrumental assistance" to "ecological integration".

items.abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. This association should be interpreted in light of the measures’ reference frames: GenAI dependency was specific to reliance on generative AI, whereas effort regulation reflected a broader academic self-regulatory tendency and perceived learning outcomes referred to recent coursework rather than a specific GenAI-supported task. The comparison of unadjusted and frequency-adjusted score-based models provided a more differentiated assessment of robustness. The negative association between GenAI dependency and effort regulation, the positive association between effort regulation and perceived learning outcomes, and the negative indirect association remained similar after adjustment for GenAI use frequency. However, the small negative total association was no longer statistically significant in the adjusted model, indicating that the evidence for this overall relationship was less robust. The change in the total coefficient was small and should not be interpreted as demonstrating that use frequency substantially explained the association. These results suggest that dependency-oriented reliance and frequency of GenAI use should be distinguished, but they do not establish their independent causal contributions to learning. Because the data were cross-sectional, the indirect association represents a statistical feature of the specified model rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. Reverse, reciprocal, and alternative directional relationships remain plausible. Moreover, the score-based sensitivity estimates should not be directly compared with the coefficients from the primary latent-variable SEM because the two approaches differ in their measurement specifications. The findings contribute to self-regulated learning research by identifying effort regulation as a specific resource-management process associated with dependency-oriented GenAI use and perceived learning outcomes. The negative indirect association suggests that learner-controlled persistence is relevant when examining students’ reliance on readily available AI assistance. However, GenAI dependency explained only 6.6% of the variance in effort regulation, indicating that other motivational, instructional, and contextual factors remain important. The distinction between dependency and frequency of use further suggests that frequent GenAI engagement should not automatically be interpreted as problematic reliance. Because perceived learning outcomes reflected students’ broader evaluations of recent coursework, these findings extend understanding of subjective learning experiences without establishing effects on task-specific or objectively assessed performance. items.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose The primary objective of the study was to determine how clinically accurate and useful ChatGPT-4o–generated outputs are when identical prompts are entered simultaneously in 3 independent ChatGPT sessions utilizing the same user-facing model. The secondary objective was to identify whether differences in outputs affect clinical outcomes (ie, impact variability). Methods Five clinical prompts focusing on diabetes management and counseling were developed. Each clinical prompt was simultaneously inputted into 3 separate devices using ChatGPT-4o to generate outputs. Through a modified Delphi technique, 5 clinical pharmacy faculty members with expertise in diabetes management independently rated each ChatGPT-generated output for accuracy (poor, borderline, or good) usefulness (not useful, somewhat useful, or very useful) and impact variability (low, moderate, or high). After initial assessment, responses were collated and anonymously shared among the pharmacy faculty raters. The faculty members were invited to revise their evaluations based on collective feedback, then convened in a virtual panel with moderators to discuss evaluations and work towards consensus. Results Consensus was achieved for all ChatGPT outputs. Accuracy ratings ranged from borderline to good. Two of the clinical prompts yielded outputs that received different accuracy ratings, which may have impacted variability. Usefulness ratings ranged from somewhat useful to very useful, with one clinical prompt yielding outputs that received different usefulness ratings. Conclusion While ChatGPT-4o outputs were generally accurate and useful, limitations and inconsistencies were noted. Users should be aware simultaneously generated outputs across multiple devices using ChatGPT can vary in their accuracy and usefulness in diabetes management.

items.abstract_text: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. items.abstract_text: Today, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is quickly becoming a staple of university students' work, as it can provide instant answers to information search, writing, explanation and problem solving. While GenAI can aid in learning, overreliance can lessen students' independent thinking. This study explores the ties between generative AI reliance and students' problem-solving skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediation factor and AI literacy as a moderation factor. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is suggested with a sample of 100 University students. The data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, regression, mediation and moderation analysis through SPSS. The conceptual model suggests that students' problem-solving ability may be linked to their degree of cognitive offloading, which could be further linked to their reliance on GenAI. The authors suggest AI literacy as a boundary condition that could affect the relationship between GenAI dependence and problem solving ability. New studies suggest that students' use of GenAI in problem-solving is multi-layered and constructive, as well as thoughtless, and that there are four aspects of AI literacy: knowledge, application, evaluation, and understanding of ethical issues. Thus, the present study is centered on not only students' usage of GenAI, but also how reliance on GenAI can impact their thinking processes when addressing academic challenges.

reading.limitations: There are some constraints to be taken into account. The first is that a cross-sectional design cannot make causal inferences. Second, a response bias can occur in self-reported measures. The study thus offers a specific educational psychology approach for studying GenAI dependence in university education, as well as cognitive offloading and problem-solving.

items.abstract_text: Background As Taiwan enters a super-aged society, the prevalence of dementia continues to rise, highlighting the need for scalable, noninvasive approaches to identify behavioral alterations associated with cognitive decline. AI-based analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses has emerged as a potential digital phenotyping tool, but its feasibility for assessing cognitive performance remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to examine the feasibility of using AI-derived spontaneous affective facial response metrics, including affective expression congruency and onset latency, to characterize differences across cognitive performance levels in older adults with healthy cognition (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia. Methods A total of 60 participants (HC, MCI, and dementia; 20 per group) were presented with positive and negative emotion-eliciting videos and completed Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) recall and calculation tasks. Facial expressions were video-recorded and analyzed using a convolutional neural network–based AI system. AI-derived metrics included affective expression congruency, categorized as congruent, neutral, or incongruent according to the detected facial response, and affective expression onset latency, defined as the time from stimulus presentation to the emergence of a nonneutral facial expression detected by the AI model. Group differences were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA, Pearson chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise post hoc comparisons, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and education, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses. Results Affectively congruent responses were generally less frequent among participants with lower cognitive performance. During the 14-second positive stimulus, congruent positive expressions were observed in 65% (13/20) of HC participants, 20% (4/20) of MCI participants, and 0% (0/20) of participants with dementia. During the 48-second negative stimulus, congruent negative expressions were observed in 60% (12/20) of HC participants compared with 5% (1/20) of both MCI and dementia participants. Onset latency differed significantly across groups for the 14-second positive stimulus (F2,57=19.63; P<.001; η2=0.41), 52-second positive stimulus (F2,57=4.25; P=.02; η2=0.13), 48-second negative stimulus (F2,57=15.61; P<.001; η2=0.35), and MMSE-based cognitive-task condition (F2,57=11.28; P<.001; η2=0.28). After adjustment for age and education, the group effect remained significant for all latency outcomes (F2,55=3.89-10.68; all P≤.03; partial η2=0.12-0.28). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses showed stronger separation in several HC vs MCI and HC vs dementia comparisons, whereas MCI vs dementia comparisons showed limited separability. Conclusions AI-assisted analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses revealed differences in expression congruency and onset latency across cognitive performance levels. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-derived facial behavioral metrics may serve as noninvasive adjunctive features for observational cognitive assessment. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory design, modest sample size, and absence of internal or external validation.

items.abstract_text: {'en': 'Generative artificial intelligence has entered the translation workflow faster than evidence about its effect on the translator has accumulated. This study asks whether working from a large language model draft lowers cognitive load or merely redistributes it. Thirty-six translators, twenty translation trainees and sixteen practising professionals, rendered nine English popular-science and technical passages into Chinese under three within-subject conditions. These were unaided human translation (HT), post-editing of a static neural machine translation draft (NMT-PE), and post-editing of a GPT-4o draft with an interactive prompt pane (GAI-PE). Pupil diameter change, fixation duration, gaze distribution, keystroke logs, NASA-TLX ratings and MQM scores were recorded. GAI-PE cut task time by 44.2 per cent against HT and by 17.1 per cent against NMT-PE. Its MQM scores were higher than those of NMT-PE, while the difference from HT did not reach significance. Pupil diameter change was nevertheless largest in GAI-PE at 0.095 mm, against 0.083 mm in HT and 0.064 mm in NMT-PE, while gaze on the source text fell to 38.3 per cent, the lowest of the three. Subjective ratings moved the other way and ranked HT as the most demanding condition. In an exploratory analysis, self-reported AI-use frequency was associated with a smaller pupil response in GAI-PE, whereas English proficiency showed no such association. These observations are consistent with an increased demand for verification, though the generative condition also gave access to an interactive prompt pane, so the differences cannot be attributed to the model alone.'}

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have made their way into English Language Teaching (ELT) contexts, yet their pedagogical value remains contested. While many learners engage with GenAI primarily as a quick hack for producing answers, fewer use it as a resource for reflective language learning. This study explores prompt writing as a language learning task that supports both language development and metacognitive awareness. The study was conducted with a target group of pre-seminary, tertiary-level learners with mixed linguistic proficiency. Over the course of four instructional sessions, the study used a classroom-based action research design. Learners engaged in cycles of prompt drafting, GenAI-generated responses, peer discussion, and prompt refinement. Classroom observations, learner reflections, and group discussions were used to gather qualitative insights. The findings indicate measurable improvement in learners’ autonomy, as learners became aware of how lexical choices shape meaning, along with increased engagement, teamwork, and reflective thinking. The study argues that prompt writing, when treated as a language task rather than a technical skill, can function as a practical tool for fostering metacognition in ELT classrooms.

items.abstract_text: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow.
